source.title: Ensembling Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Soham U. Gadgil; Chris Lin; Su-In Lee

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE feature recovery and feature stability in language-model activations using ensemble methods, rather than testing the original toy-model superposition setup or its geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper trains sparse autoencoders on language-model activations and evaluates reconstruction, feature interpretability, and stability. It does not test whether features are nearly orthogonal, whether sparsity or importance changes their geometry, or whether LLM features are distributed across neurons. The reconstruction and AutoInterp results bear indirectly on V4; the reported stability comparison bears on the stability component of V5. Results for concept detection, spurious-correlation removal, and other downstream benchmarks are not included as rows because their task scores do not directly measure the representational claims. The flattened intrinsic-metric table was not used for connectivity or per-model stability values where its layout did not support reliable assignment.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE methods paper, and most results compare its own ensembles with baselines. It does, however, report seed-to-seed feature stability for standard base and expanded SAEs on three LMs. Stability is well below 1, and much lower for larger SAEs. That bears on the stability part of V5. Reconstruction cannot speak to V4, because base-SAE explained variance was a hyperparameter selection target (about 90%).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two corrections. The authors conclude that SAE ensembles (naive bagging, boosting) improve reconstruction, coefficient diversity and stability over an expanded SAE of matched size, and help downstream concept detection and spurious-correlation removal. However, naive bagging reconstructs worse than the expanded SAE on GELU-1L and Pythia-160M, and downstream gains depend on the method and task. The authors also flag the extra compute cost.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes SAE bagging and residual boosting on language-model activations and evaluates reconstruction, interpretability, stability, and downstream tasks; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method or measure feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with SAE method and model. The authors report different reconstruction and AutoInterp results across models and methods, and describe stability as method-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Ensembling 8 SAEs (bagging or residual boosting) improves reconstruction and stability over base and expanded SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining multiple SAEs recovers more of the activation space than one SAE of matched size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: SAE sparsity is imposed by the training architecture, so the results do not independently establish naturally sparse model features. Reconstruction and AutoInterp scores do not verify recovery against ground-truth features. Stability is reported in a qualitative aggregate statement here; the extracted intrinsic-metric table has flattened entries that do not support reliable per-model assignment for every metric.
record.rows_left_out: Concept-detection, spurious-correlation-removal, and other downstream benchmark rows were omitted because their task scores measure application performance rather than the representational claims directly. No rows were omitted from the extracted reconstruction and AutoInterp results.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: no neuron-spread measure and no ground-truth recovery. Reconstruction is a selection target, and AutoInterp has no control.
Completeness and canonicality are not measured directly; only stability across seeds is.

missing.what: Per-model stability values for base and expanded SAEs (base 0.705/0.677/0.581; expanded 0.372/0.204/0.268; ensembles 0.63–0.75).
Qualitative finding that later boosting SAEs learn additional, more specific interpretable features from the residual of earlier SAEs. This hints that a single SAE's dictionary is incomplete.

record.verdict_notes: Methods paper. Only the stability of standard SAEs bears on the claim (V5). The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped: base explained variance was tuned to about 90%, and AutoInterp has no control. The V5 verdict rests on Table 1 numbers that the rows lack.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The study tests SAE reconstruction and interpretability on selected language-model activations, but not feature spread across neurons, ground-truth feature recovery, or whether the recovered features are naturally sparse rather than sparse because of the SAE training objective.
The study measures feature stability across training runs, but does not test whether SAE features are complete or canonical units of the model representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GELU-1L, Pythia-160M, and Gemma 2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature stability across training runs for expanded and ensembled SAEs.
rows.measure: Feature stability across runs; higher values indicate more similar features across runs
rows.value: The authors state that expanded SAE stability is typically less than half the stability of ensembled SAEs.
rows.note: This qualitative aggregate statement measures stability but does not establish completeness or canonicality.
rows.check: The value should carry the numbers: max-cosine stability across 5 seeds. Base SAEs score 0.705 (GELU-1L), 0.677 (Pythia-160M) and 0.581 (Gemma 2-2B). Expanded SAEs score 0.372, 0.204 and 0.268 (Table 1, Supp. Table 1). The row should be split per model and method.

relationships.condition: Standard single SAEs (ReLU/TopK/JumpReLU) on GELU-1L, Pythia-160M L8 and Gemma 2-2B L12, compared across 5 seeds
relationships.reason: Base-SAE stability is 0.58–0.71 and expanded SAEs fall to 0.20–0.37, so features are not reproducible across seeds, especially at larger size (r28; numbers from Table 1/Supp. Table 1 text).
relationships.display_finding: Stability across five seeds was 0.58–0.71 for base SAEs and fell to 0.20–0.37 for expanded SAEs, so features were not reproducible across seeds, especially at larger sizes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The study reports SAE reconstruction metrics and AutoInterp scores for SAE-derived features, providing indirect evidence that sparse dictionaries can recover useful, interpretable structure in these activations; AutoInterp results are in r19–r27 and reconstruction results in r1–r18.
